draft.title: Using brackets
card: Brackets are a pair of curved marks, ( and ). They hold extra information inside a sentence.
The extra information can be a date, a short explanation or a small detail. Example: Our school was built in 1962 (the year my grandmother was born).
Take the brackets and the words inside them out, and the sentence must still make sense. Here that gives: Our school was built in 1962.
Use brackets for a small extra detail. The main message of the sentence belongs outside them.
draft.remember: Brackets hold extra detail, and the sentence still works without it.

a.q: Which sentence uses brackets correctly to add extra information?
opts: Our dog Biscuit (a brown kelpie) loves the beach
Our dog Biscuit (loves the beach) a brown kelpie
Our dog (Biscuit) (a brown) kelpie loves the beach
Our dog Biscuit loves (the) beach a brown kelpie
a.why: The words in brackets, a brown kelpie, are extra detail, and the sentence still works without them. In the second option the brackets hold the main action, and removing it leaves a broken sentence.
a.clue: Remove the bracketed words. Does the sentence still make sense?

b.q: Priya wants to add the year of a school camp to this sentence: We went to Kangaroo Island on camp. Which version is best?
opts: We went to Kangaroo Island on camp (2023)
We went to Kangaroo Island (we went) on camp 2023
We went (to Kangaroo Island on camp) in 2023
(We went to Kangaroo Island on camp) 2023
b.why: The year is extra information, so it goes in brackets and the rest of the sentence stays whole. The third option puts the main message in brackets, so the sentence would lose its place and meaning without it.
b.clue: Only the extra detail should go inside the brackets.

a.best: Our dog Biscuit (a brown kelpie) loves the beach

b.best: We went to Kangaroo Island on camp (2023)

problems.detail: Why (a) refers to 'the second option' as the one with the main action in brackets. Options are shuffled, and in this order the second option is the correct one. The why should name the option by its words, e.g. 'Our dog Biscuit (loves the beach) a brown kelpie'.
Why (b) refers to 'the third option' by position. Options are shuffled, so this can point to the wrong option. It should quote the option instead.

The wrong options are jumbled word strings that are plainly ungrammatical, such as 'Our dog Biscuit loves (the) beach a brown kelpie'. A Year 7 student can reject them without knowing how brackets work. Distractors should be grammatical sentences that misuse brackets.

check.summary: Both answers are correct and the card is accurate. Both whys point to options by position ('second', 'third'), which will not match once the options are shuffled. Question a's distractors are too obviously broken to test the idea.
